fields.title: Reestr: Channel Hits the Ceiling
fields.summary: The main channel is two-thirds saturated, and the annual plan needs approval in a month.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will go into the annual plan, and why?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager for Reestr.
fields.brief/company: Reestr is a fictional document management service for small businesses. 2,100 paying clients, subscription at 1,400 ₽ per month.
fields.brief/context: Search brings in 71% of new clients and pays off well, but available traffic is two-thirds exhausted. In a month, the annual plan will be approved: management expects to double the number of paying clients.
fields.brief/objective: Put together an acquisition and retention plan for the year.
fields.brief/constraints: Marketing budget is 12 million per year, one marketer, and a contractor. The product team is busy half the time.
fields.brief/task: Choose a plan and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Growth plan starts with churn, not budget
fields.learnTakeaway/body: As long as a third of your base leaves each year, acquisition works to replace lost clients, not drive growth—and no budget changes that. The second law of an annual plan is capacity: a channel that is two-thirds saturated grows non-linearly expensive, so a second one is built in advance, accepting worse unit economics. And long negotiations must start in Q1: their timeline cannot be compressed for any amount of money.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Task-based search: 71% of new clients, CAC 1,600 ₽, 1.5-month payback. About 65% of available traffic bought out; attempts to get more caused non-linear price increases.

Partnerships with accounting services: 12% of new clients, CAC near zero, works through two partners. Capacity unverified—there are about twenty partners in the market.

Organic & referrals: 14% of new clients.

Social media: tried a year ago, CAC 6,900 ₽ with LTV 19,600 ₽; shut down.

Small business banks: not tried. Two banks have a showcase of client services; getting featured takes 3–4 months of negotiations according to peers.

Industry blog updated irregularly: 9 posts per year.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Paying client churn: 3.4% per month. That's over a third of the base per year.

With a plan to double, current churn consumes almost half of new growth.

Share of users reaching first value (created and signed a document) in 7 days: 52%.

Early warning sign of churn is known: zero documents created in 14 days. Nobody checks these lists.

In the cancellation form, 44% select "not using it"—what stands behind this hasn't been investigated.

No win-back campaigns have ever been run.

Retention has no owner: marketing owns acquisition, product owns features, support owns replies.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
The reconciliation statement module is 80% ready, launching in two months.

It hurts most for clients with more than twenty counterparties — there are 340 such clients in the database.

Marketing proposes announcing to all 2,100 clients on launch day and sending an email blast to potential leads.

Support knows nothing about the module: no training was planned.

The price is not settled: whether to include it in the current plan or sell it separately.

No success criteria have been set.

Separately: the HR documents module, launched a year and a half ago, has 58 paying clients against the target of 300 set at launch. Supporting it costs about two people continuously.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Management expects paying clients to double in a year.

In 41% of deals, clients arrive knowing nothing about us; sales spends the first minutes explaining who we are.

Last autumn, the service was down for six hours. Clients were messaged 24 hours later, after an industry channel wrote about the outage. Twelve clients churned, four explicitly citing silence as the reason.

Incident management process is still not documented.

Competitors actively publish in accounting trade press.

12M budget: at current CAC, that's about 7,500 new clients, but only if channel capacity allows.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Build channel portfolio and establish retention ownership
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Acknowledge search ceiling, build second and third channels early, assign a retention owner, and roll out the module in waves.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Math settles the debate: at 3.4% monthly churn, doubling is impossible through acquisition alone—a third of the base leaves each year, consuming half the budget just on replacement.
Therefore, retention gets an owner and three processes: onboarding to first value (52% in 7 days), weekly tracking of users inactive for 14 days, and quarterly win-back campaigns. Over the year, churn drops from 3.4% to 2.2%.
Search is kept as is—buying past 65% capacity is more expensive than building a second channel.
Partnerships expand from two to eight accounting services: capacity untapped, CAC near zero.
Bank negotiations start in Q1 because they take 3–4 months, keeping 20% of the budget as a testing reserve.
Reconciliation module rolls out in waves to 340 high-counterparty clients with a "reconciliation in an hour" promise, trained support, and clear success criteria.
Paying clients +78% over the year—short of doubling, but achieved with half the churn.
Trade-off: goal formally missed, requiring a churn-based ROI case to defend.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Search pays off in 1.5 months—the best metric. Direct most of the budget there and max out volume.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
First few months show growth, but cost spikes non-linearly: past 65% capacity, CAC jumps from 1,600 to 4,100 ₽.
By mid-year, half the budget is gone, while client growth is half of target.
Monthly churn of 3.4% keeps eating a third of the base, resulting in near-zero net growth in the second half of the year.
No second channel built because nobody started it.
Trade-off: entire year spent pushing a single channel past its capacity limit, while the cheapest growth lever—retention—remained unowned.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Bet on a big module launch
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Reconciliation module is the news of the year. Announce to all clients and prospect database, invest in a launch campaign.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Announcing to 2,100 clients creates a spike: 380 people try the module in week one.
Support is untrained and flooded with questions they can't answer: response time triples, and some clients leave with a bad impression of the product as a whole.
Success criteria were not defined, so a month later people debate whether the launch succeeded.
The module ultimately settles with the same high-counterparty clients that could have been reached via a staged rollout.
The core problem—churn and channel ceiling—remains untouched.
Trade-off: launch managed as an event rather than a set of decisions, burning trust where learning on 40 clients was possible.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Monthly churn of 3.4% eats everything. Spend a year on retention: first value, early warning signs, win-backs.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The work is done right and delivers results: churn drops to 2.1%, share reaching first value grows from 52% to 68%.
This is indeed the cheapest growth lever, and the churn math holds up.
However, channels don't move all year: search hits capacity, partnerships stay at two out of twenty, bank negotiations aren't started—and they take 3–4 months.
The company enters the next year with fixed retention but no second acquisition channel.
Trade-off: right priority taken to an extreme; zero-cost upfront negotiations should have been started in advance.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Acquisition plan relies on a single channel without reserve or capacity knowledge
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Retention reduced to mechanics instead of processes with an owner and metric
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Launch reduced to an announcement date without decisions on segment, promise, and success
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Business unit closure lacks a plan for offboarding people and data
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: External communication evaluated by incoming requests and unprepared for bad news
